_doc: PseudoIR v2 Tier-1 operator registry. DATA, not code. Each op row: id, signature, semantic test vectors, and per-language columns. A column records how one source/target language realizes the op. Strategy rank and confirmation status are filled by the probers (parse prober -> source_binding + parse status; runtime prober -> runtime-confirmed/rejected). This file is the single source consulted by the demo pipeline.

_strategy_ranks.native: the language has a dedicated operator/syntax whose runtime semantics already match the op's vectors. example: kotlin '?:' for op.null_coalesce.
_strategy_ranks.sugar: a thin built-in shorthand that lowers to an already-present op with matching semantics, no helper needed. example: coalesce_assign 'x ??= y' as sugar for 'x = x ?? y' where both exist.
_strategy_ranks.synthetic: no dedicated operator; the op is emitted as a small inline expression built from other ops that DOES pass the vectors. example: python null_coalesce lowered to a conditional expression '(a if a is not None else b)' -- NOT 'a or b', which fails the falsy vector.
_strategy_ranks.polyfill: requires a named helper function/import emitted alongside the call site. example: a language with no inline conditional would get a helper 'def _coalesce(a,b): ...'.
_strategy_ranks.fail: the op cannot be realized in this language with matching semantics; no lowering known.
_strategy_ranks.native_limited: the language has native destructuring syntax but only for a restricted source shape, not the general op. example: go 'x, y := f()' works ONLY for multi-return functions and multi-assignment expression lists -- there is no destructuring of a single composite/tuple value, because go has no tuple type.
_strategy_ranks.native_operator: for op.overloaded_binary: the language PERMITS user-defined operator overloading, so the operator symbol is DEFINED on the user type (python __add__, kotlin `operator fun plus`, swift `static func +`, csharp `operator +`, cpp `operator+`, rust `impl Add`, dart `operator +`, ruby `def +`) and the call site `a + b` stays `a + b`, dispatching to that definition. Distinct from `native` (which is about a built-in operator on built-in types); here the NATIVE mechanism is the user's OWN operator definition on their type.
_strategy_ranks.method_call: for op.overloaded_binary: the target FORBIDS user-defined operator overloading (java, go, typescript, php), so the operator symbol lowers to a named method call on the left operand -- `a + b` becomes `a.add(b)`, `a == b` becomes `a.eq(b)`, etc., per the op's operators sub-table. Load-bearing for eq: in these targets the raw `==`/`===` on a user object is reference (identity) equality, so eq MUST be the method call and never the raw operator.
_strategy_ranks.native_macro_interp: for op.string_interp (P2): the target provides expression-embedding template syntax whose runtime semantics match the interpolation vectors (eval-once, left-to-right, coercion, escaping), but it is realized via a MACRO/format expansion rather than being intrinsic to the string-literal grammar node. example: rust format!("x={}", e). Distinguished from `native` (where the string literal itself carries the interpolation, e.g. python f-string) because a source-binding prober must look for the format! macro family, not a string_literal/interpolation node.
_strategy_ranks.native_spread: for op.spread_call (P2): the target has a first-class CALL-SITE spread token that unpacks an existing sequence into a callee's fixed-arity positional parameters, INDEPENDENT of whether the callee is variadic. example: python f(*lst), node/php f(...arr), ruby f(*arr).
_strategy_ranks.coupled_variadic_spread: for op.spread_call (P2): the target's spread token is syntactically legal ONLY when the callee's own trailing parameter is itself declared variadic; there is no independent spread-into-fixed-arity form (spreading into a fixed-arity callee is a COMPILE ERROR). example: go total(nums...) and kotlin total(*nums) are legal only because total is variadic.
_strategy_ranks.collection_literal_spread_only: for op.spread_call (P2): the target's spread token exists EXCLUSIVELY inside collection literals ([...a], [..a]) and is never legal at a function call site -- a false friend WITHIN the spread family, realizing neither op.spread_call nor a call-site unpack. example: dart [...nums] builds a List literal; dart has no call-arg spread at all.
_strategy_ranks.manual_unpack: for op.spread_call (P2): the target has NO call-site spread operator at all; the only realization for a KNOWN fixed arity is indexing the source container by hand at each parameter position (f(x[0], x[1], x[2])). No general runtime spread. example: cpp, java, csharp, rust, swift for the spread-into-fixed-arity vector.

_confirmation_status.runtime-confirmed: the lowering template was executed on a real runtime in-sandbox and passed every semantic vector.
_confirmation_status.parse-confirmed: the source binding (grammar node/token) was confirmed present by parsing a real snippet with the real tree-sitter grammar; runtime not exercised.
_confirmation_status.pending: neither runtime nor parse confirmation performed in-sandbox (e.g. no wheel/runtime available); a ready-to-run snippet is provided for host execution.
_confirmation_status.rejected: a candidate binding or lowering was tried and FAILED (wrong node type, or lowering failed a vector). kept as evidence, not hidden.

ops.meaning: if recv is null/None yield null (short-circuit, do NOT access member); else access member. Chains propagate the first null.

escalations.method_calls_through_chain: DECIDED (the owner, 2026-07-14): method CALLS through U.safe -- i.e. U.safe(x).method() -- are UNSUPPORTED BY DESIGN. Only ATTRIBUTE chains are supported (U.safe(x).a.b.unwrap(d)). The _SafeProxy in hub/U.py raises TypeError immediately and loudly on a call attempt ('_SafeProxy' object is not callable), which is the intended blessed behavior, not a gap to close. Rationale: a call-through hides a branch (the null short-circuit) inside an expression; it makes None provenance ambiguous (was the None the chain breaking, or a method that legitimately returned None?); and the result is undebuggable. The blessed form for a null-guarded method call is the explicit if-statement, written out. The community MAY propose call-through later, but only WITH semantic vectors attached that pin down the None-provenance and short-circuit semantics -- until then it stays a loud TypeError. This supersedes the earlier 'probed and recorded, deliberately not over-built' framing (decision queue item 7b) with a firm design ruling.

ops.signature: destructure(names: [n1, n2, ... nK], source: TupleLike[K]) -> declare-and-bind each ni := source[i]  (statement position)
ops.meaning: STATEMENT-POSITION op: declare K names and bind each from the i-th component of ONE source value, with the source value evaluated EXACTLY ONCE and fully before any name is bound. Fixed-arity tuple/pair unpack only (the Oracle Discipline case: `x, y = get_coordinates()`). The single-evaluation requirement is what the swap vector (`a, b = b, a`) catches: a naive sequential-assignment lowering (a = b; b = a) evaluates/binds left-to-right and corrupts the swap; a temp-tuple (or native tuple) lowering evaluates the whole RHS first and passes.
non_goals: nested patterns (e.g. `(a, (b, c)) = ...`) -- OUT OF SCOPE
dict/object/record-field destructuring (e.g. `{a, b} = obj`) -- OUT OF SCOPE

any arity that is not fixed and known at ingest -- OUT OF SCOPE (see escalation in REPORT_r2.md: how the Hub notation marks arity when the source type is opaque is a the owner decision, not settled here). RESOLUTION (2026-07-14): DECIDED: destructure sources must carry a statically-known component count via mandatory return-type annotation (Tuple[...]); opaque sources rejected at ingest.
ops.requires_statement_hoisting: TRUE for synthetic columns (java): the single source-level declare-and-bind becomes MULTIPLE target statements -- one temp declaration holding the once-evaluated source, then K accessor binds. A target with native tuple destructuring emits a single statement and needs no hoisting.

ops.signature: overloaded_binary(sym, lhs: UserType, rhs: UserType) -> UserType|bool   AND   overloaded_unary('-', operand: UserType) -> UserType
ops.meaning: an operator symbol applied to USER-DEFINED operand types resolves to a named method on the left operand's type. Structurally ONE op keyed by symbol via the operators sub-table below (add/sub/mul/div/mod/neg/eq/lt/le/gt/ge -- the the owner-approved 11-method table), not 11 separate ops. APPLIES ONLY to user-defined operand types: primitive arithmetic (int+int) is UNTOUCHED and never routed through this op -- the op exists so the Hub can define e.g. Vector2 + Vector2. Operand types are read from the MANDATORY annotations (the Oracle Discipline's full-annotation rule); there is NO type-inference pass. Where the target language permits user operator definition, the native operator is DEFINED on the type and `a + b` stays `a + b`; where the target forbids it (java/go/typescript/php), `a + b` lowers to the method call `a.add(b)`. The eq trap: `eq` is VALUE equality. In targets where the raw `==`/`===` on a user object is REFERENCE equality by default (java Object.equals-vs-== , javascript ===), the op MUST lower to the method call (`a.eq(b)`), NEVER the raw operator -- emitting `a == b` there would silently compare identities and pass/fail on object reference, not value. That is the false-friend this op's eq vector catches.

operators._doc: symbol -> method-name binding table. the owner-approved 2026-07-14. The method name is what the method_call columns emit (a.<method>(b)) and what the native_operator columns bind the language's operator-definition hook to (python __add__, kotlin `operator fun plus`, rust `impl Add::add`, etc.). neg is the sole UNARY entry (unary minus); the rest are binary.
operators._ordering_synthesis: the owner decision 2026-07-14: the ORDERING methods (le/gt/ge) are NOT author-implemented. The Hub author implements ONLY lt and eq; le/gt/ge are SYNTHESIZED from those two -- le = lt || eq, gt = !le, ge = !lt. This is why `synthesized: true` is set on le/gt/ge below and `author_implemented: true` on lt (and on eq, add, sub, mul, div, mod, neg). Rationale: a single lt+eq pair defines a strict-weak/total order; deriving the other three mechanically prevents an author from shipping mutually-inconsistent operators (the ordering-coherence risk that was previously escalated). Targets with a native three-way comparator (kotlin compareTo, rust PartialOrd, ruby <=>) MAY collapse all four onto that comparator instead of the literal lt||eq form, but the SEMANTICS are pinned to the synthesis rule above.

-u.note: unary minus (-a); spelled -u in this table to distinguish from binary subtraction which is '-'.

==.note: VALUE equality. method_call columns whose raw == is reference equality (java, typescript) MUST use a.eq(b), never ==.

<.note: the ONE author-implemented ordering method; le/gt/ge are derived from lt+eq (see _ordering_synthesis).

non_goals: operator overloading on PRIMITIVE operand types -- OUT OF SCOPE (primitive arithmetic is never routed through this op).
type INFERENCE of operand types -- OUT OF SCOPE (operand types come from mandatory annotations only).

compound-assignment operators (+=, -=, ...) on user types -- STILL BANNED (the owner decision 2026-07-14): the Hub does not accept `a += b` on a user type. Recorded blessed semantics IF this ban is ever relaxed: REBIND, i.e. `a += b` lowers to `a = a.add(b)` (build a fresh value and rebind the name), NEVER an in-place mutation of `a`. This keeps user types value-like and avoids aliasing surprises. The ban stands; the rebind rule is the pre-decided answer for the day it is lifted, so no future re-litigation.

any operator/method beyond the approved 11 -- extension policy set by the owner 2026-07-14: (a) BITWISE operators (&, |, ^, <<, >>, ~) APPROVED IN PRINCIPLE, to be added on demand (not implemented yet, no new snippets this pass); (b) INDEXING is the NEXT queued extension -- getitem/setitem only (`a[i]` read and `a[i] = v` write), with NO slice support on user types (`a[i:j]` is out); (c) matmul (@) and callable (making a user instance callable, `a(...)`) are DEPRIORITIZED -- recorded, not queued.

ordering-coherence guarantees across lt/le/gt/ge -- RESOLVED (the owner decision 2026-07-14): coherence is now GUARANTEED BY CONSTRUCTION, not left to the author. The author implements only lt and eq; le/gt/ge are synthesized (le = lt||eq, gt = !le, ge = !lt -- see operators._ordering_synthesis). Because all four derive from the single lt+eq pair, they cannot be mutually inconsistent. No longer an open escalation.

ops.signature: range(a: int, b: int, inclusive_end: bool = false, step: int = 1) -> Sequence[int]
ops.meaning: produce the integer sequence starting at a, stepping by step, stopping at or before b. inclusive_end controls whether b itself is a member: false (default, python-shaped) excludes b; true includes b when it falls on a step boundary in the step's direction. step defaults to 1 (ascending); a negative step walks descending. inclusive_end AND step are PARAMETERS of this ONE op, not separate ops -- the structural decision that makes the `..` false friend (kotlin/ruby/swift closed vs rust/python half-open) a single boolean flip rather than hidden per-language op identity. The `inclusive_1_to_5` vs `exclusive_1_to_5` pair is the trap catcher: a lowering that spells kotlin `a..b` as python `range(a,b)` without adjusting the end bound gets length 4 not 5.

parameters.inclusive_end: boolean, default false. true = b is a candidate member (kotlin `..`, ruby `..`, rust `..=`, swift `...`); false = b never a member (python range(), kotlin `until`, ruby `...`, rust `..`, swift `..<`).
parameters.step: integer, default 1. Sign+magnitude determine direction and stride. PROBED (see non_goals + REPORT_p2.md): python and rust require step sign to agree with a/b direction (mismatched sign -> EMPTY sequence, not error); ruby's plain Range has no inherent direction (reversed-bounds `a..b` iterated plainly is empty) but Range#step(-1) on the SAME object silently walks descending -- the negative-step escalation.

non_goals: float/char/generic-comparable ranges -- OUT OF SCOPE, integer-only.
lazy/infinite ranges (rust unbounded `a..`) -- OUT OF SCOPE.

whether 'descending' is direction-baked-in-at-construction (python-shaped: step sign is part of the range's identity, mismatched-sign is empty by design) or a post-hoc reversal of an ascending range (ruby step()-shaped) -- ESCALATED to the owner (REPORT_p2.md), not decided. Current vectors use the python-shaped model; both in-sandbox runtimes produce the same length/first/last under it.

ops.signature: f(*expr) / f(...expr) -- unpack expr (a sequence) into f's declared positional parameters, one element per parameter, in order
ops.meaning: unpack an EXISTING list/array/sequence into POSITIONAL call arguments at a CALL SITE. Given a fixed-arity callee f(a,b,c) and lst=[1,2,3], spreading yields f(1,2,3): the callee's OWN declared parameters each receive one unpacked element. DISTINCT from decl.variadic (xforms.json), which is a callee-side COLLECTION of loose call-site arguments into one parameter. The two compose (spread INTO a variadic parameter) without collapsing -- proven by prober/spread_variadic/demo_spread_variadic.py vector C. This is the `...`/`*` three-way false friend from REPORT.md finding 4: the SAME token is call-arg-spread here, variadic-decl in decl.variadic, and collection-literal spread in dart/csharp -- disambiguated at grammar level by node type (python list_splat at call site vs list_splat_pattern in a param list).

ops.signature: string_interp(chunks: [Chunk]) -> string  where Chunk = literal(text) | embed(expr: Any)
ops.meaning: concatenate an ordered sequence of literal-text chunks and embedded-expression chunks into one string. Each embedded expression is evaluated EXACTLY ONCE, in left-to-right chunk order, before any subsequent chunk's expression (a lowering that re-evaluates an embed, or evaluates out of order, fails the eval_once / left_to_right vectors). A non-string embedded operand (e.g. an int) is coerced to its language-native string form (Display/toString/valueOf/description) and MUST match the literal decimal representation. Literal occurrences of the language's own trigger character(s) ($, {, }, \() inside a chunk must be escapable to their literal form without triggering interpolation; the escape mechanism is language-specific and recorded per column.

ops.signature: match_expr(subject: T, arms: [{pattern, guard?: bool, result: U}], exhaustive: bool) -> U
ops.meaning: evaluate subject EXACTLY ONCE; test arms top-to-bottom; the FIRST arm whose pattern matches AND whose guard (if present) holds yields its result. `exhaustive` is a REQUIREMENT FLAG: the Hub PROPOSES (see exhaustiveness + REPORT_p2.md escalation) that every match carry a catch-all else/wildcard arm, so behavior on an uncovered subject is always well-defined regardless of the target's native stance. The exhaustiveness fork is the flagship P2 finding: the SAME non-exhaustive-match shape produces FOUR distinct outcomes across targets (compile error / silent pass-through / none-yield / runtime throw) -- see the exhaustiveness sub-object, probed and recorded, not assumed.

exhaustiveness._doc: per-language: what actually happens when a NON-exhaustive match (no catch-all arm) hits an uncovered subject value. python/ruby/typescript/cpp were EXECUTED in-sandbox (prober/match_expr/exhaustiveness_probe.out); the rest are from language semantics + the pending host snippets.
exhaustiveness.python: none-yield (statement form falls through silently, no exception, result unchanged; no dedicated match-EXPRESSION form exists)
exhaustiveness.ruby: none-yield as expression (case-as-expression yields nil) / pass-through as statement
exhaustiveness.cpp: pass-through (switch without default: silent no-op, compiles clean on a plain int)
exhaustiveness.rust: exhaustive-required (compile error 'non-exhaustive patterns', ALWAYS, statement or expression position)
exhaustiveness.kotlin: exhaustive-required as when-EXPRESSION (compile error) / pass-through as when-STATEMENT (silent no-op)
exhaustiveness.go: pass-through (switch: NO exhaustiveness check ever, missing case is a silent no-op)
exhaustiveness.java: exhaustive-required as switch-EXPRESSION (compile error) / pass-through as switch-STATEMENT (silent no-op)
exhaustiveness.csharp: exhaustive-required-soft as switch-EXPRESSION (CS8509 compile WARNING, not error) + throws SwitchExpressionException at runtime if the gap is hit / pass-through as switch-STATEMENT
exhaustiveness.php: throws \UnhandledMatchError at runtime, ALWAYS (php match is always an expression, strict-compares, no silent fallback)
exhaustiveness.dart: exhaustive-required as switch-EXPRESSION (compile error unless wildcard `_`) / pass-through as switch-STATEMENT
exhaustiveness.swift: exhaustive-required (compile error, ALWAYS -- no silent-pass-through form exists at all; the strictest of the 12)
